title: An 80-year-old woman's Apple Watch Series 3 shows her heart rate dropping from 99 to 65 beats per minute as her atrial fibrillation reverts, which a concurrent Holter monitor confirms
summary: An 80-year-old woman's Apple Watch Series 3 showed a sudden drop in heart rate from 99 to 65 beats per minute at 19:29, when a Holter monitor recorded her reversion to sinus rhythm.
account: Toner, Al-Kaisey, Koshy and Lim of the Department of Cardiology, Austin Hospital, Melbourne, published a case in BMJ Case Reports on 4 February 2020 without giving the date of the event. The journal accepted the report on 13 January 2020, so the episode took place before that date. An 80-year-old woman with known paroxysmal atrial fibrillation wore a 24-hour Holter monitor to assess rate control. On returning the monitor she reported feeling her heart “doing a flip” at 19:29. She noted that her heart rate had suddenly dropped from 99 beats per minute (bpm) to 65 bpm on her Apple Watch Series 3. The Holter showed that she had reverted from atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm at that time. The authors exported 199 watch readings over 22 hours and matched them to the Holter. The watch's average heart rate was 94 bpm in atrial fibrillation and 66 bpm after reversion. The report describes no notification, irregular-rhythm alert or electrocardiogram app. The report documents no change in her treatment. The authors declared no competing interests and no funding. In its 2018 decision on the Apple Watch Irregular Rhythm Notification Feature, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) states that the feature is not intended for people already diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. The patient read the plain heart-rate display herself, so the FDA decision does not cover this use.
purpose: Show the wearer an optical estimate of the pulse. In this case the patient read that estimate herself to time a rhythm change.
system: Apple Watch Series 3 heart-rate readings (optical photoplethysmography)

ratings.reason: The patient learned from her watch, and had confirmed by Holter, that her rhythm had reverted at 19:29. The report records no change in management, so the benefit is informational only.

ai_role.statement: No alert, notification or rhythm classifier was involved. The watch displayed a photoplethysmographic heart-rate estimate, the patient noticed the drop, and the authors compared the readings with the Holter afterwards. The paper does not describe the heart-rate estimation as machine learning. So the AI character of the contribution is not established.
